title: Kersands' jokes, the English queen, and the impostor John Johnston
summary: Love recalls Kersands' chicken joke, how he made a solemn queen laugh in England, his spending and drinking, and a big man in the show who was mistaken for him in Mississippi.

venues.name: Overton and Senior Ragtime Minstrel Show

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: Huh? Well, I don't forgot all them old jokes. They was old funny jokes anyhow, you know. He tells a guy that he known. He'd be telling the chicken about, telling the people that he didn't like chicken very much, you know. And all that kind of stuff. He said, but he'd have one on the Sunday if he had to buy one. He must have been stealing them all the time. Yeah. He said, I don't have a chicken all the Sunday if I had to steal one. If I had to buy one. He said, but I don't like chicken very much. He said, I don't like nothing about a chicken but his neck. But his head. And his neck. And the two wings. Out there, I'd say, and the back. You know, and the people would laugh. He'd let them laugh. Well, I think he was finished, you know. He'd say, and the toes. And the egg back. Oh, he'd go on down until there wasn't no more chicken. Then the people would laugh again, you know. I think he was finished. In time, you say that, and he'd stop that, you know. He'd say, I would have eat the feathers, but they're too hard to clean. He went over in England. He couldn't, there was a queen over there. Nobody couldn't make her laugh. Belka Sandshue was over there and went before the queen, you know. And they say that if he'd make her laugh, that she'd give him a fine present, you know. She was a solemn person. Oh, he'd done all his tricks. She'd pull all them vests off, you know. Louisa grabbed him and brought him on out. That wouldn't make her laugh. So they was having tea, you know. They drinks tea over in England, regular. And they had those little cups, you know. They're small. But they're too big for a person to sit in their mouth, you know. They were sitting to the table, and he done tried to make her laugh all kinds of ways. She wouldn't laugh. So they start to drink the tea, you know. He just took the cup and sauce and put it all in his mouth. They had to get a towel. She had a hysteric, man. She laughed. She give him a diamond about big as your finger there. That big diamond, gold handle, umbrella. Walk the stick with a gold knob on it. He brought that back. He gave him a lot of money, too. He sure went busted around. Let me see. Just before I got on that Overton Senior show, she told us on the show, she used to talk with we boys in the daytime. She said, Billy would spend about two, three fortunes. He would go up to the Elks' places like that, you know, all up when he'd get around New York, them big places. And he'd spend too much money and he'd drink so much until he'd be sick, you know, all the time. His wife was worried. They had a state loan on the course. She used to go out at night and pay high as $10, $15 cab fare, you know, going around looking for him. To bring him in, you see. He'd be in the Elks' place somewhere and drink a lot of champagne. He'd want to be a big shot like the rest of the fellas, you know. He'd buy too much champagne and he'd be sick all the next day. So she'd go look for him. A poor Billy would come on in. Well, we had a fella on the show called John Johnston. He was a great big fella, about six foot four. And he wore suits with big stripes, you know, a great big stripe. He used to wear fine clothes, you know. And he was so big and he looked so much different from the other fellas in Mississippi. Every time we'd go to, you know, they'd say, oh, that's Billy Cassand there, you know. And he just had to be Billy Cassand. They'd say, what's your name? He'd say, that's all right, but it's Billy. And he'd carry him on downtown the gang of fellas, you know. And give him champagne, fill his pocket up with cigar. He'd come back late at night, you know. And he'd say, you're Louisa. That's the way he'd call me, you know. What you say, Billy? Well, Louisa wouldn't let him out when we went over there in Mississippi. John Johnston, they'd take him all the time down to the Elks. He'd come back with cigars and everything. And Billy Cassand knows what he was doing, you know. Got on to what he was doing. He'd say, Louisa, I don't like that fella there. He was misrepresenting. He says, I don't like him. And we had a trombone player called Floyd Mike Miller. He used to play with the cattle band in Shreepo. He used to do it for them, man. He used to stand alongside the cars, you know. And Miss Cassand would come off. He'd get in a conversation with him, you know. And after a while, year come John, he'd light out and go downtown somewhere and get her plenty to drink, you know. Highballs and stuff like that. They think it'd be Billy Cassand. He'd come back laughing and John would laugh at him, you know. Man, this world, old man, the death. Louisa, I don't like that fella. In Florida, he'd be across the street killing himself laughing, getting his kicks, you know. Louisa.
